newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada auto union negotiators refuse to feel heat.
newsitem.headline: Canada auto union negotiators refuse to feel heat.

text.p: When Canadian Auto Workers head Buzz Hargrove last weekend likened outsourcing to crack cocaine and union negotiators wore T-shirts saying, "Outsource this!", it was clear contract talks were heating up.
But as the tense negotiations with Chrysler Corp 's Canada unit approached a midnight deadline on Tuesday, front-line union negotiators shrugged off the pressure as just another day's work.

"Why get stressed about it? It doesn't settle the contract any faster," said Rick Reaume, a member of the union's master bargaining team. "Having a cool head is probably going to help you in the long run."

Even if the CAW, which represents 12,600 Chrysler workers, strikes a deal with Chrysler, it must negotiate separate pacts with General Motors Corp 's Canadian unit and Ford Motor Co 's Canada subsidiary.

Reaume, vice-president of CAW local 444 in Windsor, Ontario, was on the CAW bargaining team in contract talks three years ago. Some of his fellow bargainers have been on the master committee since 1979 and Reaume was confident they "have the ability to get the job done, stress or no stress."
Although a possible strike is most stressful to new workers, the CAW's more seasoned leadership accepts it as a part of the territory.
The union's 20 master-level negotiators have been holed up for more than a month in a downtown Toronto hotel where the negotiations are taking place.
The hotel has attracted a swarm of press, but the attention has not ruffled the calm of the union negotiators, who lounge in the corridors between meetings, smoking and laughing.
Asked if things were heating up at the table as the strike deadline neared, one negotiator shrugged and grunted before re-entering a bargaining room.

At the union office of local 1285 outside Toronto, 12 union members on Monday assembled about 50 picket signs for the 3,000 union members represented by the local. Chairman Gerald Harvey organized a strike duty schedule for a possible strike. But he did not seem too concerned.
"We're in our regular preparatory phase," said Harvey. "It's pretty much a matter of course, same as it was last time." The 1993 contract was settled without a strike.

Despite such statements, Charlotte Yates, professor of labor relations at McMaster University in Hamilton, Ontario, believes negotiators are under immense pressure once a strike deadline has been set.
"The pressure of negotiations at this stage is always really intense. It is really is high stress," said Yates. "It's long hours...and you never know at what point you are going to push too hard."
But a CAW spokeswoman laughed off questions about stress. "So you go without sleep for a few days, so what? You just get the job done. Buzz does it all the time."

Hargrove, who negotiates dozens of contracts each year for all sectors of his giant union, fires up the rhetoric when the cameras are rolling. But he takes a pragmatic approach to the job as the strike deadline approaches.
With just hours remaining before the strike deadline, Hargrove was not even wearing a watch.
